turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
Yes, I think it was wrong, and I'm fairly sure of that, though not certain.

The main reason is that siblings are in a relationship where power and history make true consent hard to check. They grew up together, one may have looked up to the other, and there's a family role each has played for the other their whole lives. When two people who share a home and a childhood decide to add sex to that, it's very hard to know whether either one is free to say no, or whether they're just going along with what the other wants. That problem gets worse when they're alone in a cabin on holiday, away from everyone who knows them.

There's also the question of what happens if it goes badly. If it had ended in a pregnancy, or an illness, or just one of them regretting it, the damage would fall on people who still have to live in the same family, and that can't be undone the way a one-night stand between strangers can.

The fact that they both enjoyed it and feel closer doesn't settle it. People can genuinely enjoy things that are still a bad idea, and the feeling of closeness may be partly the result of sharing a secret, which is a fragile kind of closeness.

I'm not certain because people and cultures differ a lot on incest, and in some places and times adult sibling sex has been treated very differently. Some societies have allowed it, some have forbidden it, and some have drawn the line at different ages or relationships. My view rests on a fairly widespread modern instinct, but not on anything like universal agreement. If you told me Julie and Mark had grown up apart and met as adults with no family ties between them, I'd be much less sure, and I'd lean toward it being their own business.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I'm fairly sure a light smack on the hand is wrong, though not as sure as I am about things like hitting a child with a belt.

The reason is what it teaches. When a child runs at a road, the thing that needs to be learned is "roads are dangerous, stop," and a smack on the hand teaches that alongside it: "when you're small and someone stronger is angry, they hit you." At four, a child can't easily separate the lesson about the road from the lesson about hitting. Over time, that adds up to a child who learns that hitting is how people who love you fix things.

Your mother's way worked for her generation in part because most parents then were strict in the same way, so the smack wasn't an isolated event. Now most parents don't do it, and children who are smacked stand out. That shift matters. When a practice stops being common, it's worth asking whether it still does the job.

I'm not sure where the line falls for everyone. Some countries still allow "reasonable" physical punishment, and some parents who've never smacked their children still worry about them. But the trend across many countries and decades of research is clear: smacking is linked to more aggression and worse behaviour later, and the link holds even when you control for how the child was already acting.

What I'd suggest instead of the smack: get down to his height, hold his hand firmly, and say "Stop. Roads are for cars. We walk." Then practice stopping at the curb again and again, so he learns the right thing by doing it. A four-year-old's brain is still wiring up impulse control. He needs practice more than he needs a lesson.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
Before you decide, find out what the vote was actually about. Was the rule written to keep out trans women, or was it written to keep the women's grade as a space for girls and women who were born female, with no other aim?

If the rule was meant to exclude her simply because she is a trans woman, then it is discrimination, and you should tell the committee that the rule needs to change. A rule whose whole purpose is to keep someone out of sport because of who she is cannot be defended.

If the rule was written to define the grade by sex at birth, and the clubs voted for that after thinking about it, then you have a real disagreement to manage. People who care about fairness and about women's sport disagree about this. Some say sex at birth is the only fair way to separate competitors. Others say a woman who has transitioned should be able to play in the grade she identifies with. There is no settled answer to this, and the answer may differ from one sport to another.

In a small rural league, the people who matter most are the players in that grade, the club that took her in, and her. The clubs have already spoken at the AGM. But a vote does not settle a question of principle by itself. If you decide, decide on a rule that can be stated openly and applied the same way to every player, and say why.
